claim: Somatostatin-expressing (SST) neurons in the visual sector of the nRT preferentially project to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN).
source: Here, we show that somatostatin- (SST) but not parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons in the visual sector of the nRT preferentially project to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN), and modulate visual information transmission and gamma activity in primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: Supported by anatomical tracing experiments showing dense axonal boutons from SST nRT neurons in dLGN (Figure 1B-D) and retrograde labeling experiments (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).

claim: Parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons in the visual sector of the nRT do not preferentially project to the dLGN.
source: Here, we show that somatostatin- (SST) but not parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons in the visual sector of the nRT preferentially project to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN), and modulate visual information transmission and gamma activity in primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: Supported by anatomical data showing only very sparse input from PV nRT neurons to dLGN (Figure 1B-D).

claim: SST neurons in the nRT modulate visual information transmission in primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Here, we show that somatostatin- (SST) but not parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons in the visual sector of the nRT preferentially project to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN), and modulate visual information transmission and gamma activity in primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: Supported by optogenetic manipulation experiments showing changes in V1 neuronal responses and information encoding (Figures 2, 6).

claim: SST neurons in the nRT modulate gamma activity in primary visual cortex (V1).
source: Here, we show that somatostatin- (SST) but not parvalbumin-expressing (PV) neurons in the visual sector of the nRT preferentially project to the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN), and modulate visual information transmission and gamma activity in primary visual cortex (V1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological recordings showing that optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons reduces gamma power in V1 (Figure 2E, I).

claim: Selective visual attention is associated with gamma activity in the visual cortex.
source: Visual perception in natural environments depends on the ability to focus on salient stimuli while ignoring distractions. This kind of selective visual attention is associated with gamma activity in the visual cortex.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior literature on gamma oscillations and attention.

claim: The nucleus reticularis thalami (nRT) has been implicated in selective attention.
source: While the nucleus reticularis thalami (nRT) has been implicated in selective attention, its role in modulating gamma activity in the visual cortex remains unknown.
evidence: Supported by reference to existing literature on nRT function.

claim: The role of nRT in modulating gamma activity in the visual cortex was previously unknown.
source: While the nucleus reticularis thalami (nRT) has been implicated in selective attention, its role in modulating gamma activity in the visual cortex remains unknown.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: Gamma oscillations in the visual cortex are associated with a high level of cortical activity in rodents, carnivores, and primates.
source: Gamma oscillations, particularly in the visual cortex in rodents, carnivores, and primates, are associated with a high level of cortical activity, and some have speculated that they may play a causal role in perception and the focusing of attention (Gray et al., 1992; Singer and Gray, 1995; Kreiter and Singer, 1996; Yazdan-Shahmorad et al., 2013) or in enabling a time-division multiplexing of cortical responses to multiple simultaneous stimuli (Stryker, 1989).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Some have speculated that gamma oscillations may play a causal role in perception and the focusing of attention.
source: Gamma oscillations, particularly in the visual cortex in rodents, carnivores, and primates, are associated with a high level of cortical activity, and some have speculated that they may play a causal role in perception and the focusing of attention (Gray et al., 1992; Singer and Gray, 1995; Kreiter and Singer, 1996; Yazdan-Shahmorad et al., 2013) or in enabling a time-division multiplexing of cortical responses to multiple simultaneous stimuli (Stryker, 1989).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on cited literature.

claim: Two types of gamma oscillations have been reported in the primary visual cortex (V1), differentiated by whether they result from intra-cortical or subcortical inputs through the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN).
source: Two types of gamma oscillations have been reported in the primary visual cortex (V1), differentiated by whether they result from intra-cortical or subcortical inputs through the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) in the mouse thalamus (Saleem et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Saleem et al., 2017.

claim: dLGN is the source of the specific sensory input to V1.
source: dLGN—the source of the specific sensory input to V1—gates the flow of all visual information to V1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the visual pathway.

claim: dLGN gates the flow of all visual information to V1.
source: dLGN—the source of the specific sensory input to V1—gates the flow of all visual information to V1.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the visual pathway.

claim: The activity in dLGN is controlled by inputs from GABAergic neurons from the nucleus reticularis thalami (nRT).
source: The activity in dLGN is controlled by inputs from GABAergic neurons from the nucleus reticularis thalami (nRT) (Houser et al., 1980; Sherman and Koch, 1986; McCormick and Bal, 1997; Gentet and Ulrich, 2003; Lam and Sherman, 2011; Reinhold et al., 2015; Halassa and Acsády, 2016; Crabtree, 2018; Campbell et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Optogenetic activation of inhibitory (Gad2-positive) neurons in the dorsal portion of the nRT transiently reduces activity in the dLGN.
source: Indeed, optogenetic activation of inhibitory (Gad2-positive) neurons in the dorsal portion of the nRT transiently reduces activity in the dLGN (Reinhold et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Reinhold et al., 2015.

claim: Optogenetic activation of inhibitory neurons expressing somatostatin (SST) in transgenic mice reduces activity in the dLGN.
source: Similar results were obtained with optogenetic activation of inhibitory neurons expressing somatostatin (SST) in transgenic mice (Campbell et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campbell et al., 2020.

claim: It is unknown whether nRT can control gamma rhythms in V1.
source: However, it is unknown whether nRT can control gamma rhythms or the representation of visual information in V1, and if so, whether such control involves a specific cell type.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: It is unknown whether nRT can control the representation of visual information in V1.
source: However, it is unknown whether nRT can control gamma rhythms or the representation of visual information in V1, and if so, whether such control involves a specific cell type.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: Somatosensory nRT PV but not SST neurons exhibit intrinsic rhythmogenic properties due to the presence of low-threshold T-type calcium channels.
source: Specifically, we showed in mice that (1) somatosensory nRT PV but not SST neurons exhibit intrinsic rhythmogenic properties due to the presence of low-threshold T-type calcium channels; (2) PV and SST neurons in the somatosensory nRT segregate into distinct input-output circuits; and (3) PV neurons are the main rhythm generators in the somatosensory circuits.
evidence: This refers to findings from previous work by the authors (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017).

claim: PV and SST neurons in the somatosensory nRT segregate into distinct input-output circuits.
source: Specifically, we showed in mice that (1) somatosensory nRT PV but not SST neurons exhibit intrinsic rhythmogenic properties due to the presence of low-threshold T-type calcium channels; (2) PV and SST neurons in the somatosensory nRT segregate into distinct input-output circuits; and (3) PV neurons are the main rhythm generators in the somatosensory circuits.
evidence: This refers to findings from previous work by the authors (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017).

claim: PV neurons are the main rhythm generators in the somatosensory circuits.
source: Specifically, we showed in mice that (1) somatosensory nRT PV but not SST neurons exhibit intrinsic rhythmogenic properties due to the presence of low-threshold T-type calcium channels; (2) PV and SST neurons in the somatosensory nRT segregate into distinct input-output circuits; and (3) PV neurons are the main rhythm generators in the somatosensory circuits.
evidence: This refers to findings from previous work by the authors (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017).

claim: It remained unknown whether PV and SST neurons also have distinct roles in other sensory sectors of the nRT.
source: However, it remained unknown whether PV and SST neurons also have distinct roles in other sensory sectors of the nRT.
evidence: This is a statement about the state of knowledge prior to the current study.

claim: A positive relationship between gamma power and the encoding of memories as assayed by retrieval has been widely reported for many years in the hippocampus and closely related cortical areas.
source: A positive relationship between gamma power and the encoding of memories as assayed by retrieval has been widely reported for many years in the hippocampus and closely related cortical areas (Wang, 2010 and references therein).
evidence: Supported by citation to Wang, 2010 and references therein.

claim: In sensory cortex, it has not been clear whether gamma power is associated with the encoding of information.
source: In sensory cortex, however, it has not been clear whether gamma power is associated with the encoding of information (Ray and Maunsell, 2015).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ray and Maunsell, 2015.

claim: Confocal microscopy revealed dense axonal boutons from SST nRT neurons in the dLGN.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed dense axonal boutons from SST nRT neurons in the dLGN, but only very sparse input from PV nRT neurons (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: Confocal microscopy revealed only very sparse input from PV nRT neurons to the dLGN.
source: Confocal microscopy revealed dense axonal boutons from SST nRT neurons in the dLGN, but only very sparse input from PV nRT neurons (Figure 1B–D).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 1B-D.

claim: PV neurons are thought to represent the major cellular population of nRT.
source: This was surprising given that PV neurons are thought to represent the major cellular population of nRT (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017; Li et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Clemente-Perez et al., 2017 and Li et al., 2020.

claim: PV but not SST neurons from the nRT projected densely to the somatosensory ventroposteromedial (VPM) thalamocortical nucleus.
source: As previously shown, PV but not SST neurons from the nRT projected densely to the somatosensory ventroposteromedial (VPM) thalamocortical nucleus (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: PV nRT neurons projected to the higher-order visual thalamus LP.
source: Also, PV nRT neurons projected to the higher-order visual thalamus LP (Figure 1B–D, Figure 1—figure supplement 2), suggesting that lack of dense synaptic boutons in dLGN was not due to lack of expression of the viral construct in PV nRT neurons.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1B-D and Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: Injections of the retrograde tracer cholera-toxin (CTB) in dLGN resulted in retrograde labeling of SST and PV neurons in the visual sector of the nRT.
source: Furthermore, injections of the retrograde tracer cholera-toxin (CTB) in dLGN resulted in retrograde labeling of SST and PV neurons in the visual sector of the nRT (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by retrograde tracing data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: SST and PV neurons projecting to first- and higher-order visual nuclei are intermingled in the same visual sector of the nRT.
source: Nevertheless, these results suggest that SST and PV neurons projecting to first- and higher-order visual nuclei are intermingled in the same visual sector of the nRT.
evidence: This is an inference based on the retrograde labeling data.

claim: Retrograde labeling revealed neurons that co-expressed SST and PV markers.
source: Retrograde labeling also revealed neurons that co-expressed SST and PV markers consistent with previous work (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017, Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by retrograde labeling data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2 and citation to Clemente-Perez et al., 2017.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons reduced across-trial average power in all recording channels and all frequencies in V1, with the strongest reduction in the gamma band.
source: Optogenetic activation reduced across-trial average power (scaled by 1/f) in all recording channels and all frequencies, but the strongest reduction was in the gamma band (Figure 2C, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2C and Table 1.

claim: Locomotion dramatically increases power at higher frequencies in the gamma band (30–80 Hz) in V1.
source: Consistent with previous findings, locomotion itself differently modulated power across different frequencies (Niell and Stryker, 2010), and the main effect of locomotion was a dramatic power increase at higher frequencies in the gamma band (30–80 Hz) (Figure 2D, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2D and Table 1, and citation to Niell and Stryker, 2010.

claim: Activation of SST nRT neurons significantly reduced gamma power in V1, whether the mice were still or running.
source: Whether the mice were still or running, activation of SST nRT neurons significantly reduced gamma power, but not theta and beta power, in V1, compared to baseline (Figure 2E, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2E and Table 1.

claim: Activation of SST nRT neurons did not significantly affect theta and beta power in V1.
source: Whether the mice were still or running, activation of SST nRT neurons significantly reduced gamma power, but not theta and beta power, in V1, compared to baseline (Figure 2E, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2E and Table 1.

claim: Visual stimulation alone reduced theta but enhanced beta- and gamma-band LFP power compared with baseline activity in V1.
source: Visual stimulation alone reduced theta but enhanced beta- and gamma-band LFP power compared with baseline activity (Figure 2H).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2H.

claim: In the presence of visual stimulation, optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons significantly enhanced theta power while reducing power in other frequency bands in V1.
source: In the presence of visual stimulation, optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons significantly enhanced theta power while reducing power in other frequency bands (Figure 2H, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2H and Table 1.

claim: Only the reduction of gamma power by SST nRT activation was consistently observed across all four recorded mice during visual stimulation.
source: However, only the reduction of gamma power was consistently observed across all four recorded mice, while other effects were variable across subjects (Figure 2I, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2I and Table 1.

claim: NS cells consist of fast-spiking interneurons.
source: NS cells consist of fast-spiking interneurons, whereas BS cells are 90% excitatory and 10% inhibitory cells (Barthó et al., 2004; Atencio and Schreiner, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barthó et al., 2004 and Atencio and Schreiner, 2008.

claim: BS cells are 90% excitatory and 10% inhibitory cells.
source: NS cells consist of fast-spiking interneurons, whereas BS cells are 90% excitatory and 10% inhibitory cells (Barthó et al., 2004; Atencio and Schreiner, 2008).
evidence: Supported by citations to Barthó et al., 2004 and Atencio and Schreiner, 2008.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons during visual stimulation significantly suppressed activity of both BS and NS cell types in V1 of all four mice during both stationary and locomotion states.
source: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons during visual stimulation significantly suppressed activity of both BS and NS cell types in V1 of all four mice during both stationary and locomotion states (Figure 2K, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2K and Table 1.

claim: Visual stimuli evoked strong responses in all layers of V1.
source: Visual stimuli evoked strong responses in all layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B), and optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons reduced the activity evoked by visual stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons reduced the activity evoked by visual stimuli in V1.
source: Visual stimuli evoked strong responses in all layers (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A, B), and optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons reduced the activity evoked by visual stimuli (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2C, D.

claim: The changes in LFP power produced by optogenetic manipulation of the nRT neurons were not solely due to reduction in the firing rate of V1 neurons.
source: Interestingly, the changes in LFP power produced by optogenetic manipulation of the nRT neurons were not solely due to reduction in the firing rate of V1 neurons (Figure 2L, Table 1).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 2L and Table 1.

claim: Activating PV nRT neurons produced only insignificant effects on V1.
source: Indeed, consistent with their weaker projection to dLGN, activating PV nRT neurons produced only insignificant effects on V1 (Figure 2—figure supplement 3, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 3 and Figure 2—source data 1.

claim: The average change in gamma response to PV nRT activation was in the opposite direction than the effect obtained with SST nRT activation.
source: Surprisingly, the average change in gamma response to PV nRT activation, while not statistically significant, was in the opposite direction than the effect obtained with SST nRT activation (Figure 3A, Table 2).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3A and Table 2.

claim: The difference between effects of activating SST or PV nRT neurons on firing rates was parallel to their effects on gamma.
source: The difference between effects of activating SST or PV nRT neurons on firing rates was parallel to their effects on gamma (Figure 3B).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Activation of SST nRT neurons caused a robust reduction in the firing of both the thalamocortical neurons in dLGN and the excitatory and putative fast spiking inhibitory interneurons in V1.
source: Activation of SST nRT neurons caused a robust reduction in the firing of both the thalamocortical neurons in dLGN and the excitatory and putative fast spiking inhibitory interneurons in V1 (Figures 2, 7, and 8).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 2, 7, and 8.

claim: Electron microscopy reveals geniculate terminations of SST nRT neurons only on dLGN excitatory neurons.
source: Consistent with this effect, electron microscopy reveals geniculate terminations of SST nRT neurons only on dLGN excitatory neurons (Campbell et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Campbell et al., 2020.

claim: Activating SST nRT neurons alters not just the amount but also the pattern of activity across the population in V1.
source: Interestingly, activating SST nRT neurons alters not just the amount but also the pattern of activity across the population in V1.
evidence: This is inferred from the information encoding analysis showing reduced decoding accuracy even at equal spike counts (Figure 6C, F).

claim: Perturbation of PV nRT neurons did not affect the visual information encoding in V1.
source: In contrast, despite the fact that PV neurons are present in the visual portion of the nRT (see Figure 1—figure supplement 1), perturbation of their firing rate did not affect the visual information encoding in V1.
evidence: Supported by information encoding analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: Activation of PV nRT neurons increased gamma activity and firing rates in V1 cells while SST nRT neurons did the opposite.
source: For instance, activation of PV nRT neurons increased gamma activity and firing rates in V1 cells while SST nRT neurons did the opposite (Figure 3).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3.

claim: Inhibiting eNpHR-expressing SST nRT neurons at baseline increased the firing rates of BS and NS cells in V1 during running.
source: We found that inhibiting eNpHR-expressing SST nRT neurons at baseline increased the firing rates of BS and NS cells in V1 during running but the increase in gamma did not reach significance (Figure 5, Table 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 1, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5, Table 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: Inhibiting eNpHR-expressing PV nRT neurons neither significantly changed power in any of the frequency bands nor firing rates during still or running states.
source: Inhibiting eNpHR-expressing PV nRT neurons neither significantly changed power in any of the frequency bands nor firing rates during still or running states (Figure 5, Table 2, Figure 5—figure supplement 2, Figure 2—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 5, Table 2, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons markedly reduced mutual information between the neuronal responses and visual stimuli for both BS and NS cells in V1.
source: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons markedly reduced mutual information between the neuronal responses and our set of visual stimuli for both BS and NS cells in V1 (Figure 6A, D, Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by information theory analysis shown in Figure 6A, D, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Single-trial neuronal responses during locomotion were classified less accurately during optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons for grating orientation in both BS and NS cells.
source: Single-trial neuronal responses during locomotion were classified less accurately during optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons for grating orientation in both BS (98% laser-off vs. 81% laser-on, p=2e-11, Wilcoxon rank-sum test) and NS (86% vs. 58%, p=1e-13) cells (Figure 6B, E).
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 6B, E.

claim: The cortical representation of information about the visual world is reduced when SST nRT neurons are active.
source: This finding indicates that the cortical representation of information about the visual world is reduced when SST nRT neurons are active.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced decoding accuracy during SST nRT activation.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons led to lower population spike counts on average, which in turn led to reduced visual information.
source: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons led to lower population spike counts on average, which in turn led to reduced visual information (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A, B.

claim: Classification accuracy was always lower during optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons for equal population spike counts.
source: However, accuracy was always lower during optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons for equal population spike counts (Figure 6C, F, Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), and particularly so at high population spike counts.
evidence: Supported by decoding analysis shown in Figure 6C, F, and Figure 6—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons not only reduces spiking activity in V1 cells but also alters the spiking pattern, leading to a less accurate encoding of visual stimuli.
source: These findings indicate that optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons not only reduces spiking activity in V1 cells but also alters the spiking pattern, leading to a less accurate encoding of visual stimuli.
evidence: This is an inference based on the reduced decoding accuracy at equal spike counts.

claim: Nearly all of the SU and MU recordings in dLGN were effectively inhibited during the 4 s optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons.
source: Nearly all of the SU and MU recordings were effectively inhibited during the 4 s optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons (Figure 7—video 1), and field potentials recorded in dLGN showed a dramatic reduction across all frequency bands (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—source data 1), in agreement with a strong projection of SST nRT neurons to dLGN (see Figure 1; Campbell et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7—video 1 and Figure 7—figure supplement 1.

claim: Field potentials recorded in dLGN showed a dramatic reduction across all frequency bands during optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons.
source: Nearly all of the SU and MU recordings were effectively inhibited during the 4 s optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons (Figure 7—video 1), and field potentials recorded in dLGN showed a dramatic reduction across all frequency bands (Figure 7—figure supplement 1, Figure 7—source data 1), in agreement with a strong projection of SST nRT neurons to dLGN (see Figure 1; Campbell et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1 and Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons markedly reduced visual responses in dLGN, leaving only a few spikes in response to each cycle of the grating stimulus.
source: While visual stimuli evoked strong responses in SUs (Figure 7B, top), optogenetic activation markedly reduced those responses, leaving only a few spikes in response to each cycle of the grating stimulus (sinusoidal drifting gratings, 2 Hz temporal frequency, 0.04 Hz spatial frequency) (Figure 7B–D).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7B-D.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of SST nRT neurons caused only a slight, and not significant, increase in gamma activity and spiking in dLGN compared to baseline.
source: Optogenetic inhibition of SST nRT neurons, in line with our V1 recordings, caused only a slight, and not significant, increase in gamma activity and spiking in dLGN compared to baseline (Figure 7—figure supplement 2, Figure 7—source data 1).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2 and Figure 7—source data 1.

claim: Optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons increased the CV of dLGN responses.
source: Our data reveal that optogenetic activation of SST nRT neurons increased the CV of dLGN responses (Figure 7—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3A.

claim: The firing of SST nRT neurons reduces the ability of dLGN neurons to reliably report visual information.
source: These findings reveal that the firing of SST nRT neurons reduces the ability of dLGN neurons to reliably report visual information.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased CV of dLGN responses during SST nRT activation.

claim: Optogenetic inhibition of SST nRT neurons did not significantly reduce CV of dLGN responses.
source: In contrast, optogenetic inhibition of SST nRT neurons did not significantly reduce CV of dLGN responses (Figure 7—figure supplement 3B).
evidence: Supported by analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 3B.

claim: During visual stimulation, activation of SST neurons in nRT produced much stronger effects on dLGN firing of both SU and MU sites than did inhibiting them.
source: During visual stimulation, which increases the firing of dLGN neurons, activation of SST neurons in nRT produced much stronger effects on dLGN firing of both SU and MU sites than did inhibiting them (Figure 8B).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Activating nRT neurons powerfully reduces the visual input to V1.
source: These findings from optogenetic perturbation of SST nRT neurons on dLGN activity reveal that activating nRT neurons powerfully reduces the visual input to V1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the strong effects of SST nRT activation on dLGN activity.

claim: Locomotion increases both gamma power and visual responses in mouse V1.
source: Locomotion increases both gamma power and visual responses in mouse V1, and gates a form of adult plasticity (Niell and Stryker, 2010; Kaneko and Stryker, 2014; Kaneko et al., 2017; Hoseini et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The effects of locomotion on V1 are produced by a circuit operating through vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons in V1.
source: The effects of locomotion are produced by a circuit operating through vasoactive intestinal peptide (VIP) interneurons in V1 (Fu et al., 2014; Fu et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by citations to Fu et al., 2014 and Fu et al., 2015.

claim: During locomotion, when gamma power is strong in dLGN and V1, activation of SST nRT neurons reduces it.
source: During locomotion, when gamma power is strong in dLGN and V1, activation of SST nRT neurons reduces it (Figures 2, 3, and 8).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figures 2, 3, and 8.

claim: Visual responses of both excitatory and inhibitory cortical neurons were reduced to a similar extent by activation of SST nRT cells.
source: Visual responses of both excitatory and inhibitory cortical neurons were reduced to a similar extent by activation of SST nRT cells (Figure 2).
evidence: Supported by electrophysiological data shown in Figure 2.

claim: Locomotion via cortical VIP cells and SST nRT activation contribute independently to activity in V1.
source: These findings indicate that these two modulatory systems—locomotion via cortical VIP cells (Niell and Stryker, 2010; Fu et al., 2014) and SST nRT activation—contribute independently to activity in V1.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that SST nRT activation reduces gamma during both still and running states.

claim: In the somatosensory representation, SST nRT neurons receive inputs from mainly subcortical structures (central amygdala, anterior thalamus, external segment of globus pallidus).
source: In the somatosensory representation, SST nRT neurons receive inputs from mainly subcortical structures (central amygdala, anterior thalamus, external segment of globus pallidus) in contrast with PV nRT neurons that mainly receive sensory cortical inputs (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clemente-Perez et al., 2017.

claim: PV nRT neurons mainly receive sensory cortical inputs.
source: In the somatosensory representation, SST nRT neurons receive inputs from mainly subcortical structures (central amygdala, anterior thalamus, external segment of globus pallidus) in contrast with PV nRT neurons that mainly receive sensory cortical inputs (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Clemente-Perez et al., 2017.

claim: The SST nRT neurons are well positioned to exert a bottom-up regulation of visual attention.
source: We speculate that the SST nRT neurons are well positioned to exert a bottom-up regulation of visual attention.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the input patterns of SST nRT neurons.

claim: The effects of locomotion on V1 activity are regulated by cortical VIP interneurons that receive top-down inputs from higher cortical areas.
source: In contrast, the effects of locomotion on V1 activity are regulated by cortical VIP interneurons that receive top-down inputs from higher cortical areas (Zhang et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zhang et al., 2014.

claim: Sensory stimulation in the gamma range has been shown to enhance cognition in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease.
source: Sensory stimulation in the gamma range has been shown to enhance cognition in a mouse model of Alzheimer's disease (Adaikkan et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Adaikkan et al., 2019.

claim: nRT dysfunction has been implicated in attention disorders.
source: Given that nRT is involved in sensory processing and attention, and that its dysfunction has been implicated in attention disorders (Zikopoulos and Barbas, 2012; Ahrens et al., 2015; Wells et al., 2016), and given that gamma power has been associated with attention (Kim et al., 2016), we propose that SST nRT neurons could be a target for modulating visual attention.
evidence: Supported by citations to Zikopoulos and Barbas, 2012; Ahrens et al., 2015; Wells et al., 2016.

claim: Gamma power has been associated with attention.
source: Given that nRT is involved in sensory processing and attention, and that its dysfunction has been implicated in attention disorders (Zikopoulos and Barbas, 2012; Ahrens et al., 2015; Wells et al., 2016), and given that gamma power has been associated with attention (Kim et al., 2016), we propose that SST nRT neurons could be a target for modulating visual attention.
evidence: Supported by citation to Kim et al., 2016.

claim: SST nRT neurons could be a target for modulating visual attention.
source: Given that nRT is involved in sensory processing and attention, and that its dysfunction has been implicated in attention disorders (Zikopoulos and Barbas, 2012; Ahrens et al., 2015; Wells et al., 2016), and given that gamma power has been associated with attention (Kim et al., 2016), we propose that SST nRT neurons could be a target for modulating visual attention.
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the findings of the study.

claim: The perigeniculate nucleus in the carnivore and primate is thought to be the portion of the nRT related to the thalamocortical visual system.
source: The perigeniculate nucleus in the carnivore and primate is thought to be the portion of the nRT related to the thalamocortical visual system, although this is contested (Ahlsén et al., 1982).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ahlsén et al., 1982.

claim: The carnivore perigeniculate consists of inhibitory neurons that receive excitatory input from ascending thalamocortical axons of the dLGN as well as from layer 6 cells of V1.
source: The carnivore perigeniculate consists of inhibitory neurons that receive excitatory input from ascending thalamocortical axons of the dLGN as well as from layer 6 cells of V1, and they project back to inhibit the principal cells of the dLGN in a highly focused topographic fashion (Lam and Sherman, 2011; Soto-Sánchez et al., 2017; Crabtree, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lam and Sherman, 2011; Soto-Sánchez et al., 2017; Crabtree, 2018.

claim: The carnivore perigeniculate neurons project back to inhibit the principal cells of the dLGN in a highly focused topographic fashion.
source: The carnivore perigeniculate consists of inhibitory neurons that receive excitatory input from ascending thalamocortical axons of the dLGN as well as from layer 6 cells of V1, and they project back to inhibit the principal cells of the dLGN in a highly focused topographic fashion (Lam and Sherman, 2011; Soto-Sánchez et al., 2017; Crabtree, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Lam and Sherman, 2011; Soto-Sánchez et al., 2017; Crabtree, 2018.

claim: The focal projection of the nRT is consistent with the 'Searchlight' hypothesis for nRT function.
source: This focal projection of the nRT is consistent with the 'Searchlight' hypothesis for nRT function (Crick, 1984).
evidence: Supported by citation to Crick, 1984.

claim: The nRT of cats, ferrets, and monkeys contains both PV and SST cells.
source: Earlier studies have found that, as in the mouse, the nRT of cats (Oertel et al., 1983; Clemence and Mitrofanis, 1992), ferrets (Clemence and Mitrofanis, 1992), and monkeys (Graybiel and Elde, 1983; Jones and Hendry, 1989) contains both PV and SST cells.
evidence: Supported by citations to prior research in other species.

claim: In Galago senegalensis, different laminae of the visual portion of the nRT project to the dLGN and the pulvinar.
source: Interestingly, in one primate species, the Galago senegalensis, different laminae of the visual portion of the nRT project to the dLGN and the pulvinar, which corresponds loosely to the mouse LP (Conley and Diamond, 1990).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conley and Diamond, 1990.

claim: In Galago senegalensis, cells in the more medial laminae, which is rich in SST cells, project to the pulvinar, while cells in the more lateral laminae project to the dLGN.
source: Cells in the more medial laminae, which is rich in SST cells, project to the pulvinar, while cells in the more lateral laminae project to the dLGN (Conley et al., 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Conley et al., 1991.

claim: The findings in Galago senegalensis suggest a functional segregation of the roles of SST and PV cells in this species, although in the opposite direction to that found in mice.
source: These findings suggest a functional segregation of the roles of SST and PV cells in this species, although in the opposite direction to that found in mice, where the dLGN receives a more substantial projection from SST cells and LP a denser projection from PV cells.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative anatomy across species.

claim: The different outputs of SST and PV nRT neurons to primary and high-order visual thalamic nuclei may support the switching of attention.
source: We propose that the different outputs of SST and PV nRT neurons to primary and high-order visual thalamic nuclei, and the possible intra-nRT connections, may support the switching of attention as suggested for the nRT (Wimmer et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative proposal based on the anatomical findings and citation to Wimmer et al., 2015.

claim: The more potent effects of transiently silencing V1 by the activation of all nRT neurons in experiments using Gad2-Cre mice are due to the simultaneous suppression of both dLGN and LP thalamocortical neurons.
source: We speculate that the more potent effects of transiently silencing V1 by the activation of all nRT neurons in experiments using Gad2-Cre mice are due to the simultaneous suppression of both dLGN and LP thalamocortical neurons (Reinhold et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on comparison with prior work using Gad2-Cre mice.

claim: Excitation of SST nRT neurons does not silence activity in V1 but only reduces the information about the visual world that V1 carries.
source: Interestingly, excitation of SST nRT neurons does not silence activity in V1 but only reduces the information about the visual world that V1 carries.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that V1 neurons still fire but with reduced information content during SST nRT activation.

claim: The existence of mutually exclusive PV and SST neurons in the adult human nRT suggests that findings in mice may be relevant to the human brain.
source: However, the existence of mutually exclusive PV and SST neurons in the adult human nRT (Clemente-Perez et al., 2017) suggests that our findings in mice may be relevant to the human brain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the comparative anatomy between mice and humans.
